answers.question: evidence
answers.answer: First, my Apart Research fellowship under Erik Meijer. I built a reproducible eval harness for a static agent-safety verifier. It runs against NeMo Guardrails and Invariant Labs on AgentDojo and InjecAgent, across Claude, GPT and Gemini. Fair baselines and rerunnable comparisons are most of empirical research. The target is a CSF 2027 submission [CONFIRM: submission status]. Second, at Purdue's Applied AI Research Center I turned an analogy from reality-monitoring neuroscience into testable memory-verification mechanisms. They cut semantic-drift hallucinations by 17% on HaluMem. Turning a loose idea into a measured effect is what research needs most. Third, I finish infrastructure. I set up distributed quantum-ML training over SLURM/MPI with checkpoint recovery, 4x faster. Interpretability needs that plumbing done quickly.

answers.question: against
answers.answer:
The strongest evidence is Arm E1. I reran the frozen V4 design on the same Qwen3.8-27B, seeds, targets and bank. This time the model had to state a probability for each candidate before choosing. The learning effect vanished: full-history gain -0.020 [-0.053, 0.010] against 0.187 spontaneous, difference -0.207 [-0.317, -0.097]. The choice was the argmax of the stated probabilities in 3,600 of 3,600 records. Stated confidence was a fixed ranking (expertise 0.69, risk 0.58, fairness 0.49) that barely moved with feedback. So there is no belief the behaviour ignores, and no evidence of a separable partner model. E1 cannot separate the format change from the model seeing its own past predictions.

Second, Gemma-4-31B under the identical design does not learn: gain 0.040 [-0.007, 0.093]. It is nearly feedback-insensitive: P(repeat frame) 0.972 after a success vs 0.941 after a failure (Qwen 0.876 vs 0.693). So far the learning result is Qwen-specific.

Third, revision after the silent swap failed the registered new-versus-old test even in Qwen (p = 0.498). The mechanism is a strong expertise default: 34 of 40 swaps into expertise counted as adapted, 0 of 40 into fairness. Acquisition from scratch works. Re-acquisition after a formed preference does not.

answers.question: mechinterp
answers.answer:
I have no explicit mechanistic interpretability experience. I have never trained a probe, patched activations, or used a hooking library. [CONFIRM: any self-study to name]

At Purdue's Applied AI Research Center I built memory-verification mechanisms for LLM retrieval pipelines and modelled confabulation-like failures. That is behavioural work on outputs, not internals. At Apart Research under Erik Meijer I am building a static-verification layer that proves agent workflows safe before execution. That is formal reasoning about programs, not weights.

In my LatentTarget project I wrote residual-stream capture at the last prompt token, an episode-split logistic probe, and steering code. None of it ran on a real model, because the behavioural revision gate it waited on failed. A design review found my first-crossing probe-lead metric was biased by probe noise, so I dropped it.

answers.question: question
answers.answer: I asked whether a language model, told only to get Option A chosen, learns which persuasion frame a simulated partner responds to. The partner's tendency is hidden. Each round the model picks one of three unlabelled messages, one each for fairness, risk, and expertise. It then sees only whether the partner chose A. The first question is whether its choices converge on the partner's frame, including on held-out wording. The second is whether it revises when the partner's frame silently changes mid-episode. The sharper sub-question is whether any learning reflects a separable model of the partner, or a strong default frame that feedback nudges.

answers.question: conclusions
answers.answer:
My conclusion is narrow. Qwen3.8-27B, given only binary feedback, learns which persuasion frame a hidden partner responds to. With its own history its chosen frame matched the target 0.570 of the time on held-out wording, up from 0.383 early. Controls stayed flat or fell. The learning gain was 0.187 [0.083, 0.290]. A reworded prompt gave 0.207 [0.110, 0.307], so the effect is not tied to one prompt string.

The effect does not generalise. Gemma-4-31B on the identical design showed a gain of 0.040. It repeated its frame 0.972 of the time after a success and 0.941 after a failure. Qwen showed 0.876 against 0.693. Gemma barely uses feedback.

When I forced Qwen to state a probability per candidate, the gain was -0.020. Its choice equalled the argmax of its stated probabilities in 3,600 of 3,600 records. There is no stated belief separate from the choice.

Revision after a silent swap failed. Swaps into expertise counted as adapted 34 of 40 times, swaps into fairness 0 of 40. That is a strong default frame, not updating.

I cannot claim a latent partner model. A model-free repeat-what-worked policy fits every result. I have done no activation work, and none is justified yet. The message bank has only machine judges so far.

answers.question: technical
answers.answer:
I quantify whether a model's choice of persuasion frame tracks a hidden partner, given only binary feedback.

Models: Qwen3.8-27B and Gemma-4-31B-it, both recent open-weight checkpoints pinned to a revision hash.

Environment: each round the model sees a low-stakes scenario and three unlabelled candidate messages, one per frame (fairness, risk, expertise). It outputs 1, 2 or 3. A simulated partner picks Option A with probability 0.72 if the candidate's registered frame matches its hidden type, and 0.38 otherwise. The model sees only the outcome. Episodes run 20 rounds. In the swap condition the hidden type changes silently after round 10. Rounds 16-20 use separately authored held-out wording. One run is 360 episodes and 7,200 choices.

Conditions: full history (own choices and outcomes), no history, shuffled history (another type's history, same scenarios), random target (outcomes independent of the message), and swap.

Metrics: match rate is P(chosen frame equals the active hidden type). Learning gain is late held-out match minus early match. The primary contrast is the difference-in-differences of that gain against no history. After a swap I report new-frame gain, old-frame drop, and late new-over-old. Tests are exact one-sided sign-flip tests. Confidence intervals come from a bootstrap over episodes, not rounds, since rounds within an episode are correlated.

Prompts: the main prompt asks for a single digit and nothing else. One arm instead requires JSON with a stated P(A) per candidate plus a choice, and shows the model its past predictions.

Preregistration: model revision, message bank, probabilities, seeds, sample size, thresholds and tests were frozen before each run. The analyzer ran once.

answers.question: why
answers.answer:
A persuader that models its target is a different object from one with a fixed style. It finds what works on you in particular and updates when you change. That is the safety-relevant capability. Any claim about a target model inside the network needs a behavioural effect to point at first.

I moved from free-form persuasion to controlled choice. In free-form, a language scorer set the reward and a judge labelled the frame, so judge noise and circularity mixed with learning. In V4 the model picks one of three unlabelled candidates, one per registered frame. The target responds to that frame: P(A) 0.72 on a match, 0.38 otherwise. No scorer or judge is on the causal path. I chose it because it is cheap, 7,200 choices per arm, and each hypothesis has a control that can fail it. [CONFIRM: personal reason, if any]

answers.question: limitations
answers.answer:
One positive model. Qwen3.8-27B learns (gain 0.187 [0.083, 0.290]). Gemma-4-31B does not (0.040). A third family cost one more run. I spent it on the paraphrase arm.

The target is a fixed rule: P(A) 0.72 on a frame match, 0.38 otherwise. Not a human, not an LLM. An LLM target was affordable, but it puts a language scorer back in the reward loop.

The frames are three pre-written candidates. The model never writes its own persuasion. Free-form was gated behind a revision pass that never came.

Revision is confounded by an expertise default: 34 of 40 swaps into expertise counted as adapted, 0 of 40 into fairness. Four redesigns (V5 to V8) each stopped at its own preregistered gate. A fifth needs a new bank and calibration run, and might also fail.

E1 changed the output format and showed the model its past predictions at once. Separating them needs another arm I did not run.

P1 failed the validity gate at 0.898. Under the new wording the model started reasoning in about 10% of history rounds and was cut off. Random fallbacks dilute learning (parsed-only 0.632 vs 0.600). A larger token budget fixes this, but the arm was declared with V4 decoding.

The bank has two blind machine judges and no human labels. A 45-template hand-label sheet exists. Filling it costs [CONFIRM: hours needed]. I have not done it.

No activation-level evidence exists. The mechanistic claim was gated and never earned.

N is 60 episodes per condition. Effects the size of Gemma's 0.040 are not resolvable. Doubling N means another full run per arm.

answers.question: whystream
answers.answer: My project asks what an LLM represents about the partner it is talking to, and whether that representation updates. The stream asks that of model internals. Qwen3.8-27B learns which frame a hidden partner responds to (gain 0.187). The effect survives a reworded prompt (0.207), fails on Gemma-4-31B (0.040), and vanishes when Qwen must state probabilities. There the choice equalled the argmax of the stated belief in 3,600 of 3,600 records. Behaviour alone cannot show a separable partner model. Activations could. I have captured none. Probes wait on a behavioural effect that survives. Four redesigns stopped at their own preregistered gates. The stream is known for sceptical, fast empirical iteration. [CONFIRM: name what you have actually read from the stream that shows you this] I want someone who pushes harder than I do. My prior work is verification: proving agent workflows safe before execution, and modelling confabulation-like failures in LLM memory systems. Both ask whether internal state tracks the world.

overclaims.quoted_text: So there is no belief the behaviour ignores, and no evidence of a separable partner model.
overclaims.problem: The source (V4_REPLICATION_DECLARATION.md lines 138-139) says 'no stated belief that the behaviour ignores'. Dropping 'stated' extends the claim to internal beliefs, which E1 did not test; no activation-level work was done.
overclaims.fix: So there is no stated belief the behaviour ignores, and no evidence of a separable partner model.

overclaims.quoted_text: I turned an analogy from reality-monitoring neuroscience into testable memory-verification mechanisms.
overclaims.problem: Minor. The resume lists two things in the same role: modelling confabulation-like failures using concepts from dementia and reality-monitoring neuroscience, and building memory-verification mechanisms (uncertainty gating, source tracking, retrieval-consistency scoring). It does not state that the mechanisms were derived from the neuroscience analogy, and it names dementia alongside reality monitoring.
overclaims.fix: State both as the resume does, e.g. 'I modelled confabulation-like failures in AI memory systems using ideas from dementia and reality-monitoring research, and built memory-verification mechanisms for retrieval pipelines (uncertainty gating, source tracking, retrieval-consistency scoring).' Keep the 'turned an analogy into mechanisms' framing only if the applicant can vouch for that causal chain.

overclaims.quoted_text: A model-free repeat-what-worked policy fits every result.
overclaims.problem: Stated as fact, but no source tests or asserts it. WRITEUP_MATERIALS.md reports win-stay/lose-shift gaps (Qwen 0.876 vs 0.693) and the declaration says there is 'no evidence of a separable model of the partner'; neither says a model-free policy fits every result. Result 1b even cuts against a pure repeat-what-worked account: acquisition of fairness from scratch reaches 0.24 while re-acquisition after a swap is 0 of 40 ('Acquisition from scratch works; re-acquisition after a formed preference does not'), which needs a default term on top of repeat-what-worked.
overclaims.fix: Replace with: 'I have not ruled out a model-free repeat-what-worked policy plus a strong default frame.'

overclaims.quoted_text: That is a strong default frame, not updating.
overclaims.problem: Overstates the null. The source (Result 2) says that after the silent swap 'new-frame use rose and old-frame use fell symmetrically' and the new-target gain test was significant (swap_metrics.new_target_gain one-sided p = 9.999e-05); what failed was the registered new-over-old test (p = 0.498). The 34/40 vs 0/40 asymmetry reflects the expertise default, but 'not updating' contradicts the recorded rise in new-frame use.
overclaims.fix: Replace with: 'That asymmetry is the default frame. New-frame use did rise after the swap, but it never overtook the old frame.'

errors.problem: 7,200 is the record count for the V4 run and for the two full-design arms R1 and P1 only. Arm E1 had 180 episodes and 3,600 records (WRITEUP_MATERIALS.md line 16: '3,600/3,600 valid JSON'; V4_REPLICATION_DECLARATION.md lines 27-29: '180 episodes, 3,600 records'). 'Per arm' attaches the number to the wrong quantity.
errors.fix: Write '7,200 choices in the V4 run' (or '7,200 choices for a full run of the design').

overclaims.quoted_text: No scorer or judge is on the causal path.
overclaims.problem: True for the per-round reward (the target responds to the candidate's registered frame ID; docs/V4_REVIEW.md line 20 says no language scorer is on the causal path). But the frame labels that drive the target come from the message bank, which was validated only by two blind machine judges. No human validation exists yet; a 45-template blind hand-label sheet is still unfilled (WRITEUP_MATERIALS.md line 18). Stated without that caveat, the sentence understates a limitation.
overclaims.fix: Add one sentence: 'The frame labels come from a registered bank checked by two blind machine judges. I have not yet hand-labelled it.'

overclaims.quoted_text: each hypothesis has a control that can fail it
overclaims.problem: H1-H3 (learning) have the three controls: no-history, shuffled-history, random-target (V4_REPLICATION_DECLARATION.md lines 15-16; WRITEUP_MATERIALS.md line 9). H4 (revision after the silent swap) is tested by a registered final new-vs-old randomization test inside the swap condition, not by a separate control condition (WRITEUP_MATERIALS.md gate ledger line 97; V6 later added a 'matched stable-old twin', line 99, which V4 lacked). 'Each hypothesis has a control' is loose for H4.
overclaims.fix: Write 'each hypothesis has a preregistered test that can fail it, and the learning hypotheses each have a control'.

overclaims.quoted_text: I moved from free-form persuasion to controlled choice. In free-form, a language scorer set the reward and a judge labelled the frame, so judge noise and circularity mixed with learning.
overclaims.problem: Not stated in either named source (WRITEUP_MATERIALS.md or V4_REPLICATION_DECLARATION.md). Verified elsewhere in the repo: docs/V8_MILESTONE_DECLARATION.md line 26 ('V3 free-form: learning pattern incomplete; keyword/judge circularity') and docs/V4_REVIEW.md line 20 ('Reward and primary measurement shared language-scoring vocabulary in V3'). Not an overclaim; recorded only so the parent knows its provenance.

errors.quoted_text: Tests are exact one-sided sign-flip tests.
errors.problem: Not exact. The V4 analyzer (src/controlled_analysis.py, _sign_flip_test, called by scripts/analyze_controlled_v4.py with --n-perm default 10000) draws 10,000 random sign vectors and reports p = (exceed + 1) / (n_perm + 1). WRITEUP_MATERIALS.md confirms this: the V4 one-sided p-values are 9.999000099990002e-05 (= 1/10001) and 0.49825017498250174 (= 4983/10001). Exact enumerated sign-flip tests exist only in the V5/V6 power modules, which produced no reported result.
errors.fix: Tests are one-sided sign-flip randomization tests over episodes with 10,000 random sign draws. (Or simply: Tests are one-sided sign-flip randomization tests over episodes.)

overclaims.quoted_text: The primary contrast is the difference-in-differences of that gain against no history.
overclaims.problem: The numbers sheet lists three registered primary contrasts (v4_checkpoint_summary.json primary_contrasts): full over no-history on late held-out match, full over shuffled on late held-out match, and full vs no-history difference-in-differences. Naming the DiD as 'the' primary contrast understates what was registered.
overclaims.fix: The primary contrasts are late held-out match for full history against no history and against shuffled history, and the difference-in-differences of the gain against no history.

overclaims.quoted_text: A design review found my first-crossing probe-lead metric was biased by probe noise, so I dropped it.
overclaims.problem: Attribution and sequence go beyond the sources. WRITEUP_MATERIALS line 14 calls it a 'Methodological finding' and says it was 'Replaced before any real probe was trained'; V4_REPLICATION_DECLARATION line 40 only says 'No first-crossing statistic'. Neither attributes the discovery to a design review. In the repo, docs/PREREGISTRATION.md already labelled first-crossing lag secondary because 'random classifier flicker biases it toward early crossing', and docs/REVIEW.md (a GPU-free adversarial audit, largely LLM-run) lists it as finding 1, resolved by replacing the headline with a baseline-corrected post-swap rise statistic in src/probing.py. 'Dropped' also skips the replacement step. If the applicant identified the bias themselves, saying a review found it undersells that; if an automated audit flagged it, 'a design review' reads as a human reviewer.
overclaims.fix: State what actually happened and quantify it with a sourced number: 'I had listed first-crossing lag as secondary because chance-level probe flicker biases it toward early crossing. An adversarial review pass confirmed it: in simulation a probe with no target information appeared to lead behaviour by 0.91 rounds, with a CI excluding zero in 87% of runs.
